section: 1. Reproducibility Architecture & Five Substantive Verification Checks
text:
1. Reproducibility Architecture & Five Substantive Verification Checks
This reference site and companion PDF brief were initiated and reviewed by Matthew R.V. Ross using Google DeepMind’s Antigravity coding agent to execute an open-source, reproducible R (4.5.2) + Quarto (1.10) pipeline (src/00_setup_theme.R through src/05_verify_audit.R). Five concrete engineering and accounting checks anchor every calculation:

Deterministic Computation From 71 Checksummed Primary Filings: Zero dollar amounts, headcounts, or percentages come from language-model memory. Script 01_fetch_sources.R downloaded and SHA-256 hashed 71 primary public PDFs, governance memos, Colorado Legislative Council Blue Book fiscal notes, and federal/BLS API tables across CSU Office of Budgets, CSU IRP&E Fact Books, CDHE Budget Data Books (Formats 20, 25, 30 & 1100–1700), CSU System Audited Financial Statements (FY15–FY25), Colorado Office of the State Auditor (OSA) statutory NCAA Agreed-Upon Procedures reports (2516F-B, 2505F-B), BLS CPI-U (CUUR0000SA0), and Urban Institute IPEDS (2015–2023), logging exact source URLs and page/table references in data/sources_manifest.csv.
Multi-Ledger Accounting Triangulation Across Independent Entities: Every headline figure is cross-checked across independent reporting systems—reconciling CSU internal ColOBS division budgets (B2 Athletics $16.91M FY25 / $17.15M FY26) against Colorado State Auditor NCAA filings (2516F-B), Fact Book workforce tables against CDHE Formats 20, 25 & 30, Nov. 3, 2026 Colorado Blue Book fiscal notes (Amendment 87, Prop NN, Prop 137) against pre-election OSPB forecasts, and CSU System Financial Statements against U.S. Department of Education IPEDS series.
Separating E&G Function, Title Conversions & Scale Constraints:

Isolating HR reclassifications and functional roles (CDHE Formats 1100–1700 & continuous FB26): Cross-checking CDHE Format 20 and CSU_Factbook_FY26.pdf (pp. 107–112) controls simultaneously for -254.6 State Classified -> AP/Recharge conversions, 2018–19 Special/Temporary -> CCA faculty rank formalization, and where E&G Non-Classified (Admin Pro) staff actually work—establishing that total E&G workforce (+7.0%, 3,506 -> 3,752) tracked Student FTE (+6.6%), that 85.5% of E&G AP staff sit in Academic Support (484.1 FTE), Instruction (326.4 FTE staff who teach and support labs), Student Services (204.8), Research/Public Service (190.6), and Plant (50.1), and that Institutional Support general admin equals 239.1 total FTE (6.4% of E&G FTE / $47.50M, falling to 187.4 FTE in FY27 Estimate).
Testing headline cuts against $885.16M E&G and $66.0M FY28 math: Across CSU’s official FY26 E&G budget ($885.16M), B2 Athletics ($17.15M, 1.9%) + XA Debt Service ($31.86M, 3.6%) equal 5.5% of E&G (8.0% of 10-year E&G growth), and eliminating 100% of net Athletics support (~$15.57M) plus $1.43M in recent transition payouts still leaves ~76% (~$49M–$50M/yr) of the projected FY28 shortfall unresolved.

Disaggregating Non-E&G Research/Clinical/Agency Funds & Controlling Budget Transfers: Fact Book Table 123–124 isolates 69.7% (3,205.5 of 4,597.7) of FY25 Administrative Professional FTE funded outside E&G (Sponsored Programs, Other Funds, Recharge Centers, Auxiliaries—plus Prop 137’s dedicated non-E&G CSFS wildfire funds). Likewise, ColOBS division analyses control explicitly for FY19’s $41.64M aid shift (XA to P1) and FY26’s ~$111.26M pooled fringe decentralization.
Public-Record Verification & Open Programmatic Assertions (src/05_verify_audit.R): Claims across campus viewpoints are verified against primary public records—confirming the $1.10M Parsons and $325k Underwood settlements ($1.43M combined), Coach Mora’s $2.4M–$2.8M base / $1.5M UConn buyout package, zero CSU employment record tying external Title IX consultant Jeff Lamoureux to Fort Collins, and post-election Amendment 87 (+$1.972B FY28) / Prop NN (+$521M retained / -$153.1M near-term GF) impacts. Eight programmatic test groups in src/05_verify_audit.R verify all ledger balances, functional FTE identities, and fund partitions on every build.

Corrections, missing primary citations, or alternative accounting interpretations from any member of the CSU community are welcomed via github.com/matthewross07/csu_budget_context.

2. Accounting Scope & Deflation Notes

CSU System vs. Fort Collins Standalone Scope (finstmt2015–2025 vs. BDB/ColOBS/OSA):

CSU System Audited Statements combine Fort Collins, CSU Pueblo, and System/SPUR ($644.9M net tuition, 21.3% discount rate, $1,330.7M long-term debt in FY25 + $79.1M STRATA ATLAS Laser bonds issued June 26, 2025).
Fort Collins Standalone Scope comes from CDHE Format 30/20 Budget Data Books (FINAL_BDB), CSU Office of Budgets Operating Budget Summaries (ColOBS + OBS), IRP&E Fact Books (Tables 122–128), and Note 5 of Colorado OSA Report 2516F-B ($1,118.77M Fort Collins total debt, including $206.96M Athletics debt).

Real-Dollar Deflation (CPI-U, macro_cpiu_fy.csv):

Monthly BLS CPI-U All Urban Consumers (CUUR0000SA0, 2014–Oct 2026) is averaged across CSU’s July–June fiscal calendar so multi-year net tuition and debt series are evaluated in constant FY25 or FY26 purchasing power (FY27 covers Jul–Oct 2026).

title: Athletics Accounting & Long-Term Capital Debt Context
text: Placing a $75.24M gross Athletics budget alongside a $61.3M–$70.7M E&G operating gap makes it natural to ask whether restructuring or reducing Athletics could close the university’s shortfall. 3. Mandatory Cost Escalation, Compensation & Post-Election State Budget Context ($21.19M–$30.59M)
Under the Board of Governors’ three October 2026 FY28 planning scenarios (modeling 0%, 1%, and 3% state funding increases alongside matching compensation assumptions), health insurance, utilities, classified step mandates, and salary pools on a $900.98M State Appropriated / E&G base add $21.19M to $30.59M net of anticipated state support.
CSU’s October 7 memo cited Colorado’s September 2026 OSPB economic forecast of up to a -$1.5B state FY28 general-fund shortfall—driven heavily by Medicaid growth (~$600M+ in Gov. Polis’s November executive budget request)—leaving CSU’s state Fee-for-Service and COF support essentially flat at $211.05M (23.4% of State Appropriated / E&G revenue in FY27).

Three mechanisms summarize why November 2026 state tax results improve Colorado’s higher-education backdrop without closing CSU’s internal gap on their own:

Indirect General Fund Relief Under Amendment 87 (+$1.972B FY28): By replacing Colorado’s 4.4% flat income tax with graduated brackets (3.7%–8.4%, lowering taxes below $510,834 and raising them above) while rejecting Proposition 136’s 4.4% statutory ceiling, voters approved $1.972B in TABOR-exempt FY28 revenue (up to the $2.70B ballot cap estimate; $958.4M half-year in FY27). Although the Colorado Future's Account must supplement K-12 schools, health care/Medicaid, and early childhood rather than fund university E&G instruction directly, absorbing K-12 and Medicaid obligations removes much of the zero-sum General Fund squeeze ahead of HB26-1345 Results-Informed Funding in FY28. On CSU’s $211.05M state base, shifting legislative appropriations from a 0% freeze toward +3%–5% adds ~$6.3M–$10.6M/yr (~$2.11M per +1%).
TABOR Cap Flexibility vs. Near-Term General Fund Shift Under Proposition NN: Retaining $521.0M in FY28 TABOR surplus supports multi-year K-12 obligations and opens to general legislative priorities in FY 2036–37, though Blue Book Table 2 notes -$153.1M/yr moves out of General Government Purposes in FY27 and FY28 (Prop 132 fentanyl penalties also add -$8.9M FY28 / -$68.2M Yr-5 General Fund prison costs).
Dedicated CSFS Wildfire Funding (Proposition 137) Remains Separate From E&G: Retaining $175.0M in FY28 ($180.2M FY29) of sporting-goods sales tax directs up to $36.5M (FY28) and $42.8M (FY29) to CSU’s Colorado State Forest Service (CSFS)—a major boost for statewide wildfire mitigation that stays legally restricted to CSFS Non-E&G operations rather than offsetting Resident Instruction deficits.

text:
Topline Takeaway: Structural debt, executive transition payouts ($1.10M presidential + $325k provost = $1.43M one-time), and Athletics institutional support (~$15.57M/yr net operating, $206.96M bonded debt) are material components of Colorado State University’s fiscal picture. Yet on CSU’s $885.16M FY26 Education & General (E&G) budget, Athletics E&G base support (B2: $17.15M, 1.9%) and central debt service (XA: $31.86M, 3.6%) represent 5.5% of the operating budget and 8.0% of 10-year E&G growth (FY15–FY26). Eliminating 100% of net Athletics support and executive transition payouts would still leave roughly ~$49M–$50M/yr (~76%) of the projected $66.0M FY28 shortfall unresolved, pointing toward broader structural drivers: non-resident enrollment mix (-$25.0M), expiring one-time stopgaps ($15.11M), rising tuition discounting (21.3%), flat state support prior to Nov. 2026 ballot reforms (Amendment 87 / Prop NN relieve Medicaid and K-12 crowding on the General Fund though earmarked outside E&G), and cumulative per-employee compensation/benefit inflation ($33.7M/yr per 3% pool) across an E&G workforce whose total headcount scaled in line with enrollment (+7.0% E&G FTE vs. +6.6% Student FTE, FY15–FY26) while shifting toward academic/student support (+39.9%) and non-tenure-track instruction (CCA +40.6%, Tenured -13.8%).
Ahead of the Nov. 30 AAUP chapter meeting, Dec. 1 Faculty Council, and Dec. 3–4 Board of Governors meetings, this reference separates near-term FY28 operating mechanics (Ledger A) from multi-year structural context (Ledger B) using 71 archived primary public documents logged in data/sources_manifest.csv. High-level budget files cannot capture the operational value of specific campus services or teaching units; rather, these figures provide a common factual baseline across faculty, staff, deans, central administration, and the Board.

Reproducibility & Methodological Verification: This reference site and companion PDF brief run on an open-source, deterministic R (4.5.2) + Quarto (1.10) pipeline (src/00–src/05), initiated and reviewed with Google DeepMind’s Antigravity coding agent. text:
2. State Funding Limits, Nov. 2026 Ballot Reforms, Tuition Discounting & Research F&A Scope




Accounting-Adjusted E&G Division Trends (FY15–FY26), Institutional Discounting Rate, and Non-Resident Mix



Three structural revenue constraints help explain why active teaching schedules and record external grant volume do not automatically close an E&G operating gap:

Rising Institutional Tuition Discounting: In CSU System audited financial statements (audits_system_fy15_fy25), scholarship allowances increased from $114.4M (19.9% discount rate in FY15; 17.9% in FY17) to $174.1M (21.3% discount rate) in FY25. Within Fort Collins E&G budgets (bdb_real_fy17_fy27), institutional aid grew from $47.2M (FY15) to $88.5M (FY26) and $96.3M estimated for FY27, offsetting part of nominal tuition rate increases (3.5% resident / 4.0% NR / 3.5% differential in FY27).
State Funding Constraints & November 2026 Ballot Reforms: In FY27 (obs_state_approp_fy24_fy27), State Fee-for-Service ($161.60M) and COF stipends ($49.45M) supply $211.05M (23.4% of the $900.98M State Appropriated / E&G budget)—virtually flat versus FY26 ($210.94M). On November 3, 2026, Colorado voters approved Amendment 87 (graduated income tax generating an estimated +$1.972B in FY28 for K-12, health care/Medicaid, and early childhood), Proposition NN (raising the TABOR cap by $521.0M in FY28 while shifting -$153.1M from General Government Purposes into the Children’s Account), and Proposition 137 (directing $175.0M of sporting-goods sales tax into conservation/wildfire programs, including up to $36.5M–$42.8M/yr for CSU’s Colorado State Forest Service). While Amendment 87 relieves the Medicaid and K-12 crowding behind Colorado’s pre-election -$1.5B FY28 state shortfall, all three measures remain earmarked outside university E&G instruction (CSFS sits in Non-E&G agency funds).
Why Sponsored Research Grants Do Not Directly Cross-Subsidize E&G Instruction: CSU System grants and contracts reached $548.0M in FY25 (audits) and Fort Collins Indirect Cost Recovery (IDCR) reached $76.0M (obs). Federal F&A recovery only partially reimburses dedicated research compliance, startup packages, cost-share commitments, and laboratory infrastructure rather than generating discretionary cash for general undergraduate instruction.

1. Leadership Transition Payouts, Football Contracts & Personnel Record Checks

Verified Executive Settlements & Athletics Commitments

Combined FY26–FY27 Executive Transition Payouts ($1.43M One-Time Total):

Presidential Settlement ($1.10M): On Oct. 28, 2026, CSU announced President Amy Parsons’ resignation effective Dec. 31, 2026 (prior contract ran through Jan. 2028; Rick Miranda assumes Interim Presidency Jan. 1, 2027), alongside a $1.10M transition payout (due by Jan. 5, 2027, covering the remaining contract period plus roughly five additional months of salary) and a mutual non-disparagement agreement—prompting criticism from AAUP-CSU on Nov. 5 (aaupcsu.org) and student reporting in The Rocky Mountain Collegian.
Provost Settlement ($325,000): Former Provost & EVP Marion Underwood departed the role in early 2026 with a $325,000 settlement agreement documented in CSU public reporting before later becoming provost at George Mason University.
Fiscal Scale Context: Combined, the $1.425M in recent senior leadership settlements raises legitimate governance and confidentiality concerns, yet as a non-recurring expense it represents 2.2% of one year’s $66.0M FY28 operating gap and $0 in ongoing base savings.

Football Coaching Transition Package ($2.4M Starting Base): Head football coach Jim Mora Jr. was hired Dec. 1, 2025 on a 5-year contract escalating from $2.4M (2026) to $2.8M (2030), alongside a $150k signing bonus, a $1.5M UConn buyout paid by CSU, and an expanded assistant salary pool reported around $5M ahead of CSU’s Pac-12 transition. Reducing head coaching base pay alone resolves less than 4% of Ledger A, whereas overall Athletics net institutional support (~$15.57M/yr) and bonded debt ($206.96M) are examined in Athletics & Debt.



Independent Record Check: Title IX Consultant Jeff Lamoureux

Source Verification Note: Several campus emails and organizing discussions cited the hiring of Title IX investigator Jeff Lamoureux (also spelled Lamoureaux) alongside San Francisco Chronicle reporting as evidence of executive vetting lapses at CSU. Independent verification across CSU directories and public news archives does not confirm a CSU employment tie:

Public records: External Title IX consultant Jeff Lamoureux (CIXE) previously held Title IX coordination roles at universities outside Colorado (including Appalachian State University). Meanwhile, CSU’s official Office of Title IX Programs and Gender Equity leadership and staff roster—alongside The Rocky Mountain Collegian archives—does not list Jeff Lamoureux (note that a separate CSU student disability spokesperson, Anicee Lamoreaux, shares a similar surname). Separately, San Francisco Chronicle photojournalism involving CSU and Title IX in 2024–2025 covered Mountain West volleyball litigation rather than an investigator hire.
Why precision helps: Anchoring campus oversight discussions in documented local records—such as the $1.43M combined transition settlements, mutual non-disparagement clauses, B2/OSA Athletics support ($17.15M / ~$15.57M net + $206.96M debt), and functional E&G allocations (Academic + Student Support +39.9% vs. Format 1600 General Admin = 239.1 FTE / 6.4% in FY26)—keeps shared governance centered on verifiable primary facts.

Three comparative patterns emerge from IPEDS FY23:

Colorado State Funding Per FTE Trails Out-of-State Land-Grants: At $7,314 in state appropriations and grants per student FTE, CSU receives roughly half the per-student state support of Washington State ($17,679/FTE), Utah State ($16,171/FTE), and Kansas State ($15,112/FTE)—while still receiving more than 3× CU Boulder ($2,326/FTE). CSU Carried Relatively High Long-Term Debt Per FTE ($38,915/FTE): Among comprehensive R1 land-grants in this group, CSU’s $38,915/FTE ($1,118.6M FY23 IPEDS debt) exceeds Oregon State ($31,252/FTE), Kansas State ($23,638/FTE), Washington State ($21,804/FTE), CU Boulder ($20,634/FTE), Utah State ($16,632/FTE), and Iowa State ($15,507/FTE), trailing only specialized Colorado School of Mines ($106,552/FTE).
CSU’s All-Funds Staff Ratio (3.29x) Sits Mid-Pack: CU Boulder (3.93x), Kansas State (3.90x), Iowa State (3.43x), and Washington State (3.41x) all report higher non-instructional-to-instructional IPEDS headcount ratios than CSU (3.29x), reinforcing why disaggregating general-fund (E&G) functions (Format 1100 instructional staff vs. Format 1400–1500 advising/student support vs. Format 1600 general admin)—separate from externally funded research, clinical, and extension personnel—provides the clearer institutional benchmark.

section: 3. Constructive Questions Ahead of the FY28 Hybrid RCM Transition
text:
3. Constructive Questions Ahead of the FY28 Hybrid RCM Transition
In their Oct. 26, 2026 memo (alongside Faculty Fellows Rob Mitchell and Jennifer Martin), university leadership stated directly that changing the budget model will not by itself close a budget shortfall or generate new revenue. With FY27 serving as the Parallel Year ahead of July 1, 2027 implementation, campus discussions can focus productively on four areas:

Report Functional E&G Roles Transparently (Format 1400–1500 Support vs. Format 1600 General Admin): Publish clear unit-level breakdowns distinguishing college academic advisors, instructional/teaching-lab AP staff (326.4 FTE in Format 1100), student support, IT/compliance, and classified-to-AP conversions from central general administration (239.1 FTE in FY26, 187.4 estimated in FY27)—while keeping externally funded research, clinical, and extension staff (69.7% of AP FTE, plus Prop 137 CSFS funds) clearly separate.
Co-Design Transparent FY28 Hybrid RCM Rules: Publish clear parameters ahead of Dec. 3–4 BOG review covering “off-the-top” central assessments (XA Debt Service $31.86M, CSU Spur $15.00M), credit-hour allocation weights, and instructional subvention rules for foundational disciplines.
Align Long-Term Athletics & Debt Planning With E&G Capacity: Evaluate multi-year glide paths for CSU’s ~$15.6M net Athletics operating support (B2 $17.15M FY26 base) alongside prudent policies on any new bonded or internal treasury debt while general funds remain tight.
Track Net Tuition Yield Alongside Enrollment Headcounts: As campus recruits both resident and non-resident cohorts (-9.7% Dom NR UG in Fall 2026), evaluate net revenue per seat after institutional discounting ($174.1M System allowance / 21.3% discount rate) alongside gross headcount goals.
